notes.body:
The text's answer to whether a salary from the public treasury (بَيْتُ الْمَالِ) is lawful rests on **a single, decisive condition**: who administers it. If the person distributing the funds was appointed by the friends of Allah (أولياء الله), the income is lawful; if not, it is not.

In Ismaili understanding, "the friends of Allah" (أولياء الله) are not a loose description for any righteous individual. They refer **specifically to the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt** — the living, hereditary successors of the Prophet, each bearing divine authority in their own time, not by popular approval or conquest.

That authority was announced openly by the Prophet on the Day of Ghadir, when he said:

> مَنْ كُنْتُ مَوْلَاهُ فَعَلِيٌّ مَوْلَاهُ
> Whoever's master I am, Ali is his master.

**Maulana Ali became the first** guardian (وَلِيّ) after the Prophet — not simply a beloved figure, but one whose appointment came directly from Allah — and every Imam descended from him carried that same authority forward.

Think of the بَيْتُ الْمَالِ as a community trust fund: the wealth belongs to everyone, but only the **legally named trustee** can distribute it lawfully. When the Imam, or someone the Imam explicitly delegates, manages that distribution, any salary drawn from it is clean and permissible.

A tyrant who seizes the treasury distributes wealth without a divine mandate. **The legitimacy of the hand** that controls it is what matters — and that hand belongs to the Imams alone, and to those they formally authorize.

notes.quote: if it is administered according to the judgment of one appointed by the friends of God
etymology: وَلِيّ (guardian): from root و-ل-ي, meaning to be close or to follow immediately after. The nearest one — standing right beside you — is the وَلِيّ. Proximity becomes guardianship: the one who comes closest holds the right of care and command. Derived forms include مَوْلَى (master, patron) and وِلَايَة (guardianship, authority).

أولياء (friends of Allah): plural of وَلِيّ, from root و-ل-ي. The plural does not simply multiply individuals — it names a succession, a chain of those standing nearest to Allah across time, each the closest guardian in his own age.

بَيْتُ الْمَالِ (public treasury): compound of بَيْت, from root ب-ي-ت (to lodge overnight; hence a house or dwelling), and مَال, from root م-ي-ل (to incline, to lean). Wealth is literally what one inclines toward; the بَيْتُ الْمَالِ is the dwelling where that communal inclination — the community's resources — is gathered and kept.

مَوْلَى (master, patron): from the same root و-ل-ي as وَلِيّ, but carrying heavier relational weight — one who stands as master and protector. The Prophet's deliberate choice of this precise word at Ghadir made the point unmistakable: Ali stands nearest in authority and in love.
